meta.title: Amazon Doubled. He Didn't Sell. | Nick Sleep on Selling Winners Too Early
meta.author: Nick Sleep
meta.end: Quotations and ringed passages are from the Nomad Investment Partnership letters (Sleep, Zakaria and Company), with the letter period and PDF page shown. Lines marked “our note” are our own reading.
meta.description:
Why Nick Sleep didn't sell Amazon after it doubled: the invisible cost of selling winners early, why his worst mistake was a sale and not a bankruptcy, "start at 100% and work down", living through 2008, and three questions to ask before you "book profit". From the original Nomad letters.

Every ringed passage is shown on the real letter page, with the letter period and page. Lines marked "our note" are our own reading.
meta.sources:

meta.tags: nick sleep amazon costco, when to sell a stock, selling winners too early, profit booking, concentrated portfolio, opportunity cost investing, nick sleep letters, nomad investment partnership

beats.say: Imagine a batsman who scores a lovely fifty. The pitch is flat. The bowlers are tired. And he walks off, all by himself. Why? Fifty is a good score, yaar. Why take risk?

scene.q: Fifty is a good score, yaar. Why take risk?

beats.say: You'd call it madness. But this is exactly what most investors do with their best stocks. The stock doubles, and everyone around them says the same two words. Book profit.

In 2007, Nick Sleep faced that moment. Amazon's share price had doubled, and it had become a big part of his fund. He wrote that it would be easy for him and Zak to claim victory, do a high five, and sell. They didn't.

scene.find: claim victory, high five, and sell our shares in Amazon
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: Sleep believed the biggest mistake an investor can make is not buying a bad company. It's selling a great company too early. In his words, selling a Wal-Mart or a Microsoft in the early years of its growth.

scene.find: the biggest error an investor can make is the sale of a Wal-Mart
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: Here's why, in simple rupees. Mistake one. You buy a company for a hundred rupees, and it goes bust. You lose a hundred. Mistake two. You buy for a hundred, sell at two hundred, and it goes on to be worth a thousand. You missed eight hundred.

The first mistake hurts, but it's capped. You can never lose more than you put in. The second has no cap at all. And it never shows up anywhere. Sleep pointed out that missed gains go unrecorded in performance records.

scene.find: opportunity costs go unrecorded in performance records
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: It's like your school report card. It shows your marks. It never shows the rank you'd have got if you had actually studied.

scene.q: Your report card never shows the rank you could have got.

beats.say: Sleep had personal proof. He wrote that Nomad's greatest error was not Conseco, the company that went bankrupt on him. It was selling Stagecoach, the British bus company, which kept rising after he sold.

scene.find: our greatest error was the sale of Stagecoach
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: The bankrupt company cost money. The early sale cost more.

scene.q: The bankruptcy cost money. The early sale cost more.

beats.say: So why does everyone sell too early? Sleep listed the reasons, and they're painfully human. The stock has gone up, so it must be okay to sell. Other people are selling, so it must be okay for us too. Psychological mistakes, he said, not analysis.

scene.find: the stock has risen in price so it is OK to sell
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2005 · p.77

beats.say: In 2009 he added the professional reasons. Fund managers have to look active. Marketing wants new stories. And some managers sell their winners just to look diversified to clients.

scene.find: fund managers sell their winners in order to appear diversified
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2009 · p.161

beats.say: Notice what's missing from that list. The business got worse. None of these reasons are about the business.

scene.q: Missing from the list: “the business got worse.”

beats.say: In India we have an extra reason. Relatives. The moment your stock doubles, some uncle at a wedding says: beta, profit book kar lo. Uncle has never booked a profit in his life. But the advice is free, so it keeps coming.

Most funds build a holding slowly. One percent, then two, then three. So their best ideas almost never become big holdings. In 2007 Sleep suggested turning it upside down. Start at a hundred percent, and work down.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: He wasn't suggesting the whole fund in Amazon. Well, not just yet, he joked. And about Costco, back in 2004, he wrote that his first mistake might have been not buying enough.

scene.find: made his first mistake investing in Costco
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2004 · p.52

beats.say: Now the honest part. With about one sixth of the fund in Amazon, Sleep warned that results would swing more in the short term. Then he added: the volatility does not bother Zak and me one jot.

scene.q: The volatility does not bother Zak and me one jot.
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2007 · p.120

beats.say: A year later, it got tested. In 2008 Nomad fell forty-five point three percent. The world index fell forty point seven. Brutal.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2013 · p.212

beats.say: But in 2009, Nomad rose seventy-one point five percent.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2013 · p.212

beats.say: And most investors held on too. Withdrawals during the crisis were less than two percent of the fund.

scene.find: less than two percent of the Partnership
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2008 · p.154

beats.say: A year later Sleep told them that the simple decision not to redeem had earned them something like seventy percent, and counting. Sometimes the best thing you can do with a great investment is absolutely nothing. Which, for most of us, is the hardest thing in the world.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2009 · p.167

beats.say: Is the lesson never sell? No. Remember Conseco. Sleep held on too long because he didn't update his view when the business changed. So the rule isn't about the price. It's about the destination. Sell when the business stops heading where you thought. Not just because the price went up.

Next time a stock you own goes up a lot, ask three questions. One. Has the business changed, or only the price? Two. If I had the cash today, would I still want to own this business for ten years? Three. Am I selling because of analysis, or because of an uncle, a WhatsApp group, or the urge to feel smart?

scene.head: BEFORE I SELL
items: 1 · Business changed, or only the price?
2 · Would I buy it today, for 10 years?
If I had the cash today

beats.say: If the business is getting stronger, a rising price is a report card, not an exit sign.

scene.q: A rising price is a report card, not an exit sign.

beats.say: One. You never go broke booking profits. True. But you can stay small forever doing it. Two. A stock that has doubled must be expensive now. Not if the business has more than doubled in value. Three. Big holdings are reckless. They can be, if you don't understand the business. Sleep's big bets came after years of study, and he warned his investors about the bumps in advance.
One line for your friend over chai. Don't cut down the mango tree the year it finally gives mangoes.

scene.q: Don't cut down the mango tree the year it finally gives mangoes.

beats.say: Next. Sleep showed you could have paid over a hundred and fifty times Wal-Mart's 1972 share price, and still made ten percent a year. How can a great business look expensive, and still be cheap?

scene.find: over one hundred and fifty times the prevailing share price
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 30 Jun 2009 · p.162
